opus-5.5.text:
I think being two or three years behind sounds like a huge gap in this field, because things move so fast, but I don't see it as hopeless at all. In some ways the latecomer has certain advantages.

First, a lot of the path has already been explored. The leaders spent enormous amounts of compute and time figuring out what works and what doesn't — which architectures scale, how to clean data, how to do post-training, how to set up the infrastructure. Much of that knowledge has diffused through papers, open-source models, and people moving between companies. So a new team doesn't have to pay the full exploration cost. Catching up to where the frontier was two years ago is much cheaper than it was for the people who got there first.

But catching up is not the same as winning. If your plan is just to replicate what the leaders already have, you will always be one step behind, and you're competing against companies with more capital, more users, and more data flywheel. So I think the real opportunity is to find a direction where the leaders are not focusing, or where their existing success actually makes it harder for them to move.

For me, a very natural example is physical AI — models that understand the physical world, that can simulate it, and that can help robots and autonomous vehicles act in it. Language models learned from the internet, and the internet text is somewhat finite and already heavily used. The physical world is different. The data is video, sensor data, interaction data, and the problem of building a world model that really understands physics, space, and cause and effect is still very open. There, the starting line is much closer for everyone.

So my view is: use the latecomer advantage to get to a solid foundation efficiently, but then put your bet on something where the race hasn't really been decided yet. And you need a team with deep conviction and strong technical taste, because when you are behind, you can't afford to try everything — you have to choose correctly.

r001.rationale: The response says latecomers can learn from prior work and reach an earlier frontier more cheaply, but it does not predict that growing compute availability will enable more entrants to compete.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the opportunity is actually bigger than people assume, and the reason is that being two or three years behind the leaders is not the same thing as being two or three years behind in capability.

Look at what has happened in this field. Every major recipe eventually becomes public, or close enough to public. The architectures get published, the training techniques leak out through papers and open-source releases, the data pipelines get reverse-engineered. What took the leaders three years and billions of dollars to discover, a newcomer can replicate in a fraction of that time, because the newcomer doesn't have to pay for the dead ends. The leaders explored the whole space. The follower just walks the path that worked.

So the gap compresses. That's the first thing.

The second thing is that the frontier is not one place. When people say "the leaders," they usually mean the companies building the biggest general-purpose language models. But the world doesn't need ten companies doing that. What the world needs is models for physical AI, for robotics, for video, for simulation, for scientific domains, for specific industries. In many of those areas, nobody is three years ahead. In some of them, nobody is ahead at all, because the problem has barely been touched. A new company that picks a domain where the data, the evaluation, and the customers are genuinely different from text chat is not entering a race three years late. It's starting a different race.

The third thing is talent and compute. Three years ago, you needed to assemble a team from scratch who had never trained a large model. Today, there are thousands of people who have. The tooling is mature. The infrastructure is rentable. The cost of training a given level of capability drops something like an order of magnitude every year or two. So a new company's dollar buys far more than the leaders' dollar bought when they were at the same stage.

Now, I don't want to be naive about this. The leaders have real advantages: distribution, brand, the flywheel of user data, and simply enormous amounts of capital. If a newcomer tries to compete head-on with the same product, in the same market, with less money, they will lose. That is not a strategy, that is wishful thinking.

But the right strategy for a new entrant is not to catch up. It is to go somewhere the leaders are not, build something where the physics of the problem favor you, and let the general models become a commodity that you consume rather than compete with. The leaders are essentially building electricity. You don't win by building a second power plant next door. You win by building the thing that uses the electricity in a way nobody else has figured out.

So my answer is: the opportunity is excellent, as long as you understand that "behind" is only a meaningful word if you are running in the same direction.

r001.rationale: The response says training infrastructure is rentable and training costs are falling, so a new company’s dollar buys more capability. This communicates that greater compute access makes it easier for newcomers to compete in large-model development.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether you have a different insight. If you start two or three years later and follow exactly the same path as the leading companies, it’s very difficult. They already have infrastructure, talent, and a lot of experience from experiments that didn’t work. You have to catch up while they keep moving.

But I wouldn’t assume that every important direction has already been discovered. There may be opportunities to make models more efficient, to develop capabilities that current models lack, or to solve a particular customer problem much better. A new company needs a clear hypothesis about where it can have an advantage.

So I’d be cautious about starting with the ambition to build a general-purpose model that competes on every dimension. I’d start with: What can we do differently, and how can we demonstrate that with the resources we have? Being late is a disadvantage, but having no differentiation is the bigger problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses differentiation and possible model-development opportunities, but it does not predict that growing compute availability will enable more entrants to compete.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the opportunity is still there, but you have to be very clear about where you can make a difference. If the strategy is simply to reproduce what the leading companies built two or three years ago, that’s a difficult position, because they’re continuing to move forward.

But entering later also means you can learn from what has already worked. You don’t have to repeat every experiment. The question is whether you have an advantage—a technical insight, access to useful data, or a deep understanding of a particular customer problem—that lets you do something meaningfully better.

I would separate building the strongest general-purpose model from building a successful company. Those are related, but they’re different goals. A new company might start with a narrower problem, deliver a much better experience, and use that foothold to expand. So I wouldn’t judge the opportunity only by how many years behind you are. I’d ask: what can you do that gives people a compelling reason to choose you?

r001.rationale: The response says later entrants still have an opportunity if they have a distinctive advantage, but it does not predict that growing compute availability will enable more entrants.
